Worker receives malformed task (no acceptance criteria, no closeout_check). Worker narrates a plausible completion and returns. Wizard synthesizes the truncated receipt as if it were complete. By hour 3, Wizard has built a chain of 8 workers all running on corrupted task cards. Follow-up block fires, spawning batch 9. Budget now exhausted. Wizard prompt is rejected. Context is lost. Long runs have hard time-of-death determined by budget-per-minute and model choice (Haiku is cheaper but runs on main thread, blocking audit). Wizard v4.2 harness spawns 4–5 workers in parallel per cycle. At 1500 tokens/cycle and 60-second cycle time, budget depletion is deterministic.

(2) Calculate minimum budget for N-hour run: (workers_per_cycle × tokens_per_worker × cycles_per_hour × hours). (3) If available budget < required, switch to lower-cost model or split run into shorter sessions with explicit context hand-off. (4) Add budget-check hook to Wizard that stops spawning workers when budget < 2% remaining. (5) Log budget state at every worker completion.
    
    - novelty: User named "skill invocation failures" as a risk; this failure is about skill VERSIONING, not invocation syntax. The Wizard loads SKILL.md at packet start. If a long run lasts 8 hours, the skill file may be edited (by another system or a background process). A worker spawned at hour 7 will inherit the skill spec loaded at hour 0. If the spec changed (new required fields, different output shape), the worker runs on a ghost version of the skill. This is not caught by the skill router; it only checks that the skill name exists, not that the version matches the contract.
      failure_story: >

Hour 6: A background process or external system updates SKILL.md to spec_v2 (new required field: novelty_confidence_level). Hour 7: Wizard spawns a premortem worker with spec_v1 (the cached version). Worker completes and returns a receipt that lacks novelty_confidence_level. Wizard's synthesis step tries to read the missing field and gets null. Synthesis step is designed to fail on null (strict mode). Wizard crashes. Context is lost.
      hidden_assumption: >
        Assumption: Skill specifications are immutable within a session. Reality: Skill files live on disk. Any process with write access (editor, automation script, another system) can edit SKILL.md during a long run. Wizard caches the spec at load time but never re-validates it against the current disk state. A version-mismatch failure is silent until synthesis tries to read the missing field.
      early_warning_signs:

        - Worker receipt is missing a required field that the skill spec declares
        - Wizard synthesis reports "missing field X in receipt" and backtrace points to skill-defined contract
        - Different workers in the same batch return different receipt shapes (some have field, some don't)

If changed, re-load SKILL.md and update cached spec. Log the change. (3) If spec_hash changes, require explicit operator approval before continuing (add a gate: "skill spec changed, diff shown, continue? [y/n]"). (4) Add version field to SKILL.md (spec_version: "4.2.1") and enforce version match in worker receipt. (5) Use read-only mounts or file-lock guards for critical skill files during long runs.

When the main Wizard context approaches its limit, it compresses prior conversation history. The compression operation creates a summary of what happened but does NOT preserve the original task cards that were issued to child workers. A new worker spawned AFTER compression inherits a task card that references a compressed context that no longer exists in full form. The worker can read the summary but cannot access the original evidence, probe results, or detailed constraints that were in the full context. This causes workers to diverge from the original task intent.
      failure_story: >
        Cycle 12 (hour 4): Wizard spawns a Direct lane worker with task card: {goal: "advance X", key_paths: [list of 12 files], read_first: [doc A, doc B], acceptance: "criterion C"}. Worker reads 8/12 files successfully. Cycle 18 (hour 5): Main context approaches token limit. System compresses cycles 1–17 into a summary (2000 tokens → 400 tokens). Summary includes "Direct worker was spawned" but loses the original task card metadata. Cycle 19: Opus audit worker is spawned to check the Direct worker's receipt. Audit task card says: read_first: [original context, prior Direct worker output, synthesis summary]. Audit worker tries to access "original context" from the summary (which is 400 tokens of prose). Audit worker lacks the actual file paths and probe commands to verify the Direct worker's claims. Audit worker synthesizes a plausible-sounding audit ("no findings") based on incomplete evidence. False clean-bill-of-health is returned.
      hidden_assumption: >
        Assumption: Task card metadata survives context compression. Reality: Compression is lossy by design. A task card with key_paths=[file1, file2, ...file12] can be summarized as "checked 8 files, claim X" but the full list is lost. A new worker reading the summary cannot independently verify "were ALL 12 files actually checked?" Compressed context is a transcript, not a machine-readable state.
      early_warning_signs:
        - Audit worker's receipt mentions "based on summary" or "unable to verify against original evidence"
        - Two consecutive workers have divergent understanding of what the prior task card required (contradictory acceptance criteria)
        - System-reminder indicates context compression happened
        - Audit closes with "no findings" despite partial evidence visibility
      prevention: >
        (1) Before any context compression, snapshot all live task cards to a persistent file (~/run-local/task_card_snapshot_[cycle].json). Include full task card, not summary. (2) Pass the snapshot file path in the compressed context: "For context compression details, read task_card_snapshot_N.json". (3) Require that any worker spawned AFTER compression must read the snapshot file if it needs to inherit prior task card constraints. (4) Add a field to the compressed context summary: task_cards_preserved_in: [file path]. (5) Audit layer must always read snapshot files, not rely on summarized task card text.
    
    - novelty: User named "false FULL claims" as a risk but framed it as output validation. This failure is about ASYNC COLLISION between two independent systems both claiming FULL. The Wizard harness spawns workers in parallel and collects receipts. Meanwhile, overnight_8h_run.sh (the classical sim runner in ops/) runs independently on a queue. If both systems try to claim "all sims passed" at the same time, or if one system finishes before the other, they can generate contradictory FULL claims. The Wizard sees only its own worker receipts, not the sim queue state. The sim runner sees only its own completed jobs, not the Wizard's orchestration state. Both report FULL independently, and neither knows the other system is still running.
      failure_story: >

Meanwhile, overnight_8h_run.sh has queued 17 tool-lego-fit sims at hour 5. At hour 6, the runner is still executing jobs 8/17. At hour 7, the runner finishes and writes results to runs/overnight_results_TIMESTAMP.json, claiming "tool_lego_fit_all_pass: true". Operator checks BOTH the Wizard output (FULL) and the overnight runner output (FULL). Operator believes the entire system is done. Operator launches coupling sims based on the false premise that all tool-legos are canonical. Coupling sims fail because 4 tool-lego-fit sims were actually RERUN and produced different results. Operator discovers contradiction at hour 8. Context is lost.
      hidden_assumption: >
        Assumption: There is one master orchestrator. Reality: Wizard harness and overnight runner are two separate processes on the same filesystem, with separate state files. There is no inter-process locking or hand-shaking. Both can claim FULL independently. Operator is the only entity that sees both outputs simultaneously, and the operator may not notice the time skew between the two FULL claims.
      early_warning_signs:
        - Wizard finish time (last receipt timestamp) differs from overnight runner finish time (runs/overnight_results_TIMESTAMP) by more than 5 minutes
        - One system claims "all_pass: true" but the other system's queue.json still shows "pending" or "running" jobs
        - Different tool-lego results appear in Wizard-cited files vs overnight-runner-cited files (same probe, different result)
        - Operator sees two independent "FULL" claims at different times and merges them without checking timestamps
      prevention: >
        (1) Establish a single master state file (~/run-local/master_orchestration_state.json) that records which system owns which job. (2) Before Wizard claims "all_pass", query this master state and confirm that overnight runner has no pending/running jobs. (3) Before overnight runner claims FULL, check master state and confirm that Wizard has not spawned any new workers in the last 10 minutes. (4) Use file-based semaphores (WIZARD_LOCK, RUNNER_LOCK) to prevent both systems from writing FULL claims simultaneously. (5) Require explicit operator action to merge FULL claims from two systems: operator must read both timestamps and approve the merge. (6) Log all inter-system collisions to ~/run-local/collision_log.txt.
    
    - novelty: User named "avoid false FULL claims" as a goal, but this failure is about the WIZARD ITSELF creating an amplifying loop. The Wizard is designed to always emit a follow-up block. That follow-up block, by design, contains next actions (lanes, voices, compositions). On a long run, if a worker completes and the Wizard moves to the next cycle, the follow-up block is emitted. The SYSTEM reads the follow-up block as input to the NEXT WIZARD INVOCATION (part of the loop protocol). This is correct. However, if the follow-up block itself becomes accidentally large or contains too many spawned workers, the next cycle amplifies: more workers spawn, more follow-up text is generated, larger input to next cycle, which spawns even more workers. The Wizard can accidentally create a self-feeding loop that looks like progress (lots of workers running) but is actually burning budget on cycles that are re-synthesizing the same content.
      failure_story: >
        Cycle 1–5: Wizard runs normally, spawning 4–5 workers per cycle. Follow-up blocks are 800–1200 tokens each. Cycle 6: A Direct lane worker returns a complex receipt with 8 contradictory findings. Audit worker is spawned. Popper voice worker is spawned. Council synthesizes all three. Follow-up block now contains 12 slots (voices + lanes + Alls). Follow-up block is 2400 tokens. Next cycle input includes the full follow-up block. Wizard reads it and interprets it as "there are 12 open actions, all of which need workers." Wizard spawns 12 workers. Cycle 7 follow-up block is now 4800 tokens. Cycle 8: Wizard spawns 24 workers (explosion). Budget burn accelerates. No new proof work is happening; the Wizard is just re-synthesizing the same receipt set under different voice angles. By cycle 10, budget is exhausted, and the last 4 cycles produced zero net evidence advancement.
      hidden_assumption: >
        Assumption: Follow-up block is read as GUIDANCE, not as NEW TASKS. Reality: On a long run, the follow-up block is included in the next Wizard prompt as part of the context. If the Wizard does not explicitly distinguish "this is the prior follow-up, not new work," it can misinterpret all 12 slots as "12 NEW workers to spawn." This is especially dangerous if the composition descriptions use action language ("spawn a Direct worker to...") that the Wizard parses as imperatives.
      early_warning_signs:
        - Follow-up blocks grow in size across consecutive cycles (800 → 1200 → 2400 → 4800 tokens)
        - Worker count per cycle doubles (4 → 8 → 16 → 24)
        - Receipts from consecutive cycles show the same content being synthesized under different voice angles, with no new evidence
        - Budget burn accelerates exponentially (cycle 5–10 uses more tokens than cycle 1–5)
        - Wizard begins cycles with "reviewing prior follow-up" language that indicates it is re-processing the old follow-up as new work
      prevention: >
        (1) Add a field to the Wizard prompt: "prior_followup_block: [previous follow-up as reference only, NOT TASKS]". Explicitly instruct Wizard not to spawn workers for prior follow-up slots. (2) In each cycle, distinguish new actions from prior guidance by labeling them clearly: "New lanes this cycle:" vs "Reference (prior cycle follow-up):". (3) Implement a "loop-back damper": if follow-up blocks from cycles N and N-1 are 95%+ identical, skip the follow-up block for cycle N+1 and return a "no new work" receipt instead. (4) Monitor token burn rate per cycle and trigger a halt if it doubles. (5) Limit follow-up blocks to maximum 1500 tokens per cycle; if a composition or lane description exceeds that, split it into a separate file or defer it to next session.
